content.thinking:
The user just asked to “change the building UI to be more Robloxy?” I’ve already responded by overhauling the studio editor UI: I rewrote `studio.js` to implement a full pro‑editor layout with a ribbon toolbar, explorer panel, gizmos, snap controls, etc. Then I added the missing icons to `icons.js` and updated the main CSS in `site.css` to style the new UI elements. After that I performed a quick syntax check on the rewritten JavaScript files and confirmed there were no syntax errors.

Now I need to verify that the new UI actually works in the browser. The previous steps were all static code changes; the next logical step is to run an automated end‑to‑end test that exercises the new editor features: creating a place, placing parts via the toolbox, selecting parts through the explorer, moving and scaling with gizmos, using undo/duplicate, filtering the explorer, toggling snap, checking keyboard shortcuts, and confirming real‑time collaboration with a second editor. This mirrors the comprehensive checks we performed earlier for the three‑player gameplay verification, but now focused on the studio UI.

To do this I should create a dedicated Playwright test script that can be executed on the CI server. I’ll write the script to a temporary location (`/tmp/glint-studio-ui.js`) so it doesn’t interfere with the source tree and can be run independently. The script will:

1. Launch Chromium (using the same Chrome binary we used for other tests) in headless mode.
2. Register a new user, navigate to the studio, and create a new place.
3. Capture the generated game ID from the URL for subsequent API calls.
4. Verify that the UI elements I added are present (ribbon with 4 tool buttons, 12 part palette entries, explorer rows, status bar part count).
5. Place a block via the toolbox and confirm the part count increments on the server.
6. Select the block via the explorer and ensure the properties panel shows position inputs.
7. Activate the move gizmo, locate a grab handle by probing the canvas cursor style, drag the handle, and verify the part’s X coordinate changed and snapped to 0.5‑unit increments.
8. Activate the scale gizmo, similarly locate a grab handle, drag to resize, and confirm the scale values changed.
9. Test undo twice and verify the geometry returns to the original three parts.
10. Test duplicate and check that a fourth part appears.
11. Use the explorer filter to narrow results and verify the count.
12. Toggle snap off/on and confirm the UI reflects the state.
13. Use keyboard shortcuts (1 for select, 3 for scale) and verify the active tool changes.
14. Open a second browser context, sign up a second editor, add them as a collaborator via the API, load the same place, and verify the collaborator chip appears.
15. Have the second editor place a part and ensure the first editor’s explorer updates live.
16. Take screenshots of the final studio UI and of the gizmo after moving a part for visual verification.
17. Collect any page errors or console errors, report them, and exit with a non‑zero status if any failures occurred.

All of these steps are necessary to prove the UI is functional and “Robloxy”. I’ll embed a small helper `ok` function to tally passes/fails and print a summary at the end. The script will also include error handling to crash with a clear message if anything unexpected happens.

Given the pattern of previous testing scripts, I’ll follow the same structure: define `signup`, `partsOf`, launch the browser, create contexts `ctxA` and `ctxB`, and use Playwright’s locator API for element interactions. I’ll also need to fetch the game data via the `/api/games/:gid` endpoint, passing the session cookie.

Now I just need to issue the `Write` tool call to create this script with the exact content I’ve just constructed. This will allow the test to be run later, and the user can see the screenshots and pass/fail output. So I’ll output a `Write` call targeting `/tmp/glint-studio-ui.js` with the full script content.
